glosses: gerund of verwarnen
to caution, admonish, to warn of punishment or other negative consequences
to book, to show a yellow card to (but sometimes also used for a verbal warning, which is more properly called ermahnen)
(vor D) предостерегать (кого-л. от чего-л.); предупреждать (кого-л.)
юр. сделать предупреждение (кому-л. как применение меры административного или дисциплинарного взыскания)
Admonester, avertir, mettre en garde.

examples.text: Arbeitgeber dürfen ihre Arbeitnehmer verwarnen, wenn diese ein Fehlverhalten gesetzt haben.
examples.translation: Les employeurs sont autorisés à avertir leurs employés s'ils commettent une faute.

glosses: jemanden unter Androhung einer Strafe ermahnen, streng zurechtweisen

examples.text: Weil er am Rande eines Prozesses um den gewaltsamen Tod seines Bruders einen Zeugen misshandelt hat, ist ein 19-jähriger Schüler am Montag in Frankfurt verwarnt worden.
"Ein Spieler wird verwarnt, wenn er Kopf oder Gesicht mit einer Maske oder Ähnlichem bedeckt", heißt es im offiziellen Regelheft des Deutschen Fußball-Bundes (DFB).
Arbeitgeber dürfen ihre Arbeitnehmer verwarnen, wenn diese ein Fehlverhalten gesetzt haben.
Weitere 1240 Radfahrer wurden verwarnt, weil sie auf Radwegen in der falschen Richtung fuhren.

"Im vorliegenden Fall ist ein Irrtum des Schiedsrichters nicht ersichtlich, vielmehr hat er regelkonform entschieden", heißt es in der Urteilsbegründung: "Gemäß Regel zwölf der Fußballregeln ist ein Spieler zu verwarnen, wenn er sein Hemd auszieht oder an einem Zaun hochklettert, um einen Treffer zu feiern."

translations.source_sense_description: transitiv: jemanden unter Androhung einer Strafe ermahnen, streng zurechtweisen

glosses: To make (someone) aware of (something impending); especially:
To make (someone) aware of impending danger, evil, etc.

examples.text: We waved a flag to warn the oncoming traffic about the accident.
I phoned to warn him of the road closure.

glosses: To make (someone) aware of (something impending); especially:
To notify or inform (someone, about something).

examples.text: I warned him he'd be getting a huge box of birthday presents from me.

glosses: To make (someone) aware of (something impending); especially:
To summon (someone) to or inform of a formal meeting or duty.

examples.text: The sheriff warned her to appear in court.
Committee being warned these following were absent or short …
The people had been invited to the funeral, or warnt, by a special messenger a few days before the funeral took place.
[...] the plaintiff fraudulently warned the meeting for November 15, giving only five days' notice [...]

glosses: To make (someone) aware of (something impending); especially:
To make a sound (e.g. clicking or whirring) indicating that it is about to strike or chime (an hour).

examples.text: Hark! the clock is warning ten;
No, not a word more, Andrew; the clock has warned for nine, and I am off.

The clock warned, and the hands pointed to a few minutes before the hour. The preacher looked towards it. "And, as you sit here," he cried," the Old Year is dragging out its last moments and the New Year is coming up —"

glosses: To caution or admonish (someone) against unwise or unacceptable behaviour.

examples.text: Don't let me catch you running in the corridor again, I warn you.
He was warned against crossing the railway tracks at night.

glosses: To advise or order to go or stay away.

examples.text: A sign warns trespassers off/away from the site.

glosses: To give warning.

examples.text: then Iames Cephas and Iohn [...] agreed with vs that we shuld preache amonge the Hethen and they amonge the Iewes: warnynge only that we shulde remember the poore.
She is his deepest innocence in spaces of bough and hay before wishes were given a different name to warn that they might not come true [...].
She warned that he was seriously thinking of withdrawing his offer to part the waters, ‘so that all you'll get at the Arabian Sea is a saltwater bath [...]’.
Every country has its resident experts who warn that imported television will destroy the national consciousness and replace it with Dallas, The Waltons, Star Trek and Twin Peaks.

translations.source_sense_description: transitiv: jemanden unter Androhung einer Strafe ermahnen, streng zurechtweisen

glosses: Prudence when faced with, or when expecting to face, danger; care taken in order to avoid risk or harm.

examples.text: act with caution
proceed without due caution
take caution
have caution
exercise great caution
utmost caution is required when travelling in this dangerous neighbourhood
In way of caution I must tell you.
[...] and on the Saturday heavy seas pounded the W.R. on its exposed coastal stretch between Dawlish and Teignmouth, loosening the ballast and forcing trains to proceed with extreme caution.

glosses: A careful attention to the probable effects of an act, in order that failure or harm may be avoided.

examples.text: The guideline expressed caution against excessive radiographic imaging.

glosses: Security; guaranty; bail.

examples.text: The Parliament would yet give his majesty sufficient caution that the war should be vigorously prosecuted.

glosses: One who draws attention or causes astonishment by their behaviour.

examples.text: Oh, that boy, he's a caution! He does make me laugh.
‘You are a caution,’ she said, when she came out. ‘I don't understand you.’

glosses: A formal warning given as an alternative to prosecution in minor cases.
A yellow card.
To warn; to alert, advise that caution is warranted.

examples.text: In its May 1965 issue, Life magazine condemned skateboards as a “menace to limb and even to life,” and cautioned readers about riders who “take over the paths made for peaceful strollers.”

glosses: To give a yellow card

translations.source_sense_description: transitiv: jemanden unter Androhung einer Strafe ermahnen, streng zurechtweisen

glosses: A collection of sheets of paper bound together to hinge at one edge, containing printed or written material, pictures, etc.

examples.text: Knowing I lou'd my bookes, he furniſhd me / From mine owne Library, with volumes, that / I prize aboue my Dukedome.

I repeat: it suffices that a book be possible for it to exist. Only the impossible is excluded. For example: no book can be a ladder, although no doubt there are books which discuss and negate and demonstrate this possibility and others whose structure corresponds to that of a ladder.

I can be anything.
Take a look!
It's in a book:
A reading rainbow.

Trefusis's quarters could be described in one word. Books. Books and books and books. And then, just when an observer might be lured into thinking that that must be it, more books... Trefusis himself was highly dismissive of them. ‘Waste of trees,’ he had once said. ‘Stupid, ugly, clumsy, heavy things. The sooner technology comes up with a reliable alternative the better... The world is so fond of saying that books should be “treated with respect”. But when are we told that words should be treated with respect?’
She opened the book to page 37 and began to read aloud.
He was frustrated because he couldn't find anything about dinosaurs in the book.

glosses: A long work fit for publication, typically prose, such as a novel or textbook, and typically published as such a bound collection of sheets, but now sometimes electronically as an e-book.

examples.text: I have three copies of his first book.
“I would never read a book,” he once told an interviewer. “I don’t want to say no book is ever worth reading, but I actually do believe something pretty close to that.”

They read some books
Sharing their moods
They know everything
Whatever it can mean

glosses: A major division of a long work.

examples.text: Genesis is the first book of the Bible.
Many readers find the first book of A Tale of Two Cities to be confusing.

glosses: A record of betting (from the use of a notebook to record what each person has bet).

examples.text: I'm running a book on who is going to win the race.

glosses: A bookmaker (a person who takes bets on sporting events and similar); bookie; turf accountant.
A convenient collection, in a form resembling a book, of small paper items for individual use.

examples.text: a book of stamps
a book of raffle tickets
a book of matches (matchbook)

glosses: The script of a musical or opera.

examples.text: The guild helps ensure that the ownership and control of the music, lyrics, and book of a show remain in the hands of its authors and composers—not the producers.

glosses: Records of the accounts of a business.
A book award, a recognition for receiving the highest grade in a class (traditionally an actual book, but recently more likely a letter or certificate acknowledging the achievement).
Six tricks taken by one side.
Four of a kind.
A document, held by the referee, of the incidents that happened in a game.
A list of all players who have been booked (received a warning) in a game.

examples.text: Celtic captain Scott Brown joined team-mate Majstorovic in the book and Rangers' John Fleck was also shown a yellow card as an ill-tempered half drew to a close.

glosses: The list of mares that a stallion will breed in a given season.
A list of the races that a jockey is scheduled to ride in.
The twenty-sixth Lenormand card.
Any source of instruction.
The accumulated body of knowledge passed down among black pimps.

examples.text: The Book is an oral tradition of belief in The Life that has been passed down from player to player from generation to generation.
On the other hand The Book is an oral tradition containing the rules and principles to be adopted by a pimp who wishes to be a player.

glosses: A portfolio of one's previous work in the industry.

examples.text: Getting your book (portfolio) organised is the first step, and knowing both what to include, and what to leave out, is an essential step towards achieving that important agency placement.
Your portfolio — your book — has to be killer.

glosses: The sum of chess knowledge in the opening or endgame.

examples.text: The opposite-colored bishops endgame is usually a book draw.
A book move
out of book
White to move and win. How can he do it? The BK plans a march to h8, eating the f4 pawn en route, for a book draw.
This seems certain to simplify into a battle between White's king, rook and two pawns against Black's king and rook. In some cases a book draw is possible. But a book win is more likely.

glosses: A package of silk.

examples.text: This machinery was provided with a rotary drum with received upon its periphery the "books" of silk to be operated upon and presented them to travelling, combing, or dressing surfaces. The books were clamped and released automatically by the aid of bars formed with wedges and put in operation by screws […]

glosses: To reserve (something) for future use.

examples.text: I want to book a hotel room for tomorrow night.
I can book tickets for the concert next week.
I haven't booked, so I don't have a clue as to whether the service will be busy or not. Supposedly, reservations are compulsory, but I want to find out what would happen if you just turn up.

glosses: To write down, to register or record in a book or as in a book.

examples.text: They booked that message from the hill.

glosses: To add a name to the list of people who are participating in something.

examples.text: I booked a flight to New York.

glosses: To record the name and other details of a suspected offender and the offence for later judicial action.

examples.text: The police booked him for driving too fast.

glosses: To issue a caution to, usually a yellow card, or a red card if a yellow card has already been issued.
To travel very fast.

examples.text: He was really booking until he passed the speed trap.

glosses: To record bets as bookmaker.
To receive the highest grade in a class.

examples.text: The top three students had a bet on which one was going to book their intellectual property class.

glosses: To leave.

examples.text: He was here earlier, but he booked.

glosses: simple past of bake

translations.source_sense_description: transitiv: jemanden unter Androhung einer Strafe ermahnen, streng zurechtweisen

glosses: Faire une sévère réprimande à quelqu’un, sans condamner, mais en avertissant de ne pas recommencer.

examples.text: Puis comme le vin les grisait, ils se mirent à frapper sur les bouteilles avec des couteaux. De temps à autre une femme en robe de soie bruissante se levait de table, et les admonestait.
Le garde se contentait d’admonester les coupables, et dénonçait aux parents ceux-là seuls qui étaient coutumiers de laisser aller leurs vaches en maraude.

À qui prendrait à son compte le mot de M. de Boureuille je riposterais que le talent, pour un chef, c’est de modérer les impétuosités des jeunes hommes en les admonestant doucement, sans les décourager par des paroles de glace.
Le Pacha ne put retenir son sourire devant ces farces enfantines. Il reprit son expression la plus sévère pour admonester les deux femmes.

Alors elles les mettent en demeure elles les admonestent elles leur mettent les couteaux sous la gorge elles les intimident elles leur montrent le poing elles les fustigent elles leur font violence elles leur font part de tous leurs griefs dans le plus grand désordre elles jettent çà et là le brandon de la discorde elles provoquent des dissensions entre eux elles les divisent elles fomentent des troubles des émeutes des guerres civiles elles les traitent en ennemi.

glosses: Faire une remontrance, un blâme, à huis clos à un justiciable, avec défense de récidiver.

examples.text: Le dimanche 17 décembre 1595, l'assemblée des terriers et des maîtres des métiers, désignés le 14 décembre, est admonestée par le procureur de la ville pour qu'elle choisisse des personnes idoines.

Si la contravention est établie, le tribunal pourra soit simplement admonester le mineur, soit prononcer la peine d'amende prévue par la loi. Toutefois, les mineurs de treize ans ne pourront faire l'objet que d'une admonestation.

glosses: Reprendre quelqu’un avec autorité, lui reprocher sa faute.

examples.text: Je l’ai fortement réprimandé sur sa conduite. Je l’en ai réprimandé.
Il ne peut souffrir d’être réprimandé. Quel droit a-t-il de vous réprimander ?
Nos parents, trop malades pour nous réprimander, nous laissaient déambuler à loisir.

translations.source_sense_description: transitiv: jemanden unter Androhung einer Strafe ermahnen, streng zurechtweisen

glosses: Conseiller la circonspection ; avertir d'un risque.

examples.text: […] il était très facile, même en France au milieu des années 70, de trouver des chercheurs mettant la communauté scientifique en garde contre la démonisation de cette discipline, démonisation déjà considérée comme un dérapage (Dorozynski ; Renaud).

Il a fallu la faiblesse de nos démocraties pour ne pas vouloir entendre tous ceux qui mettaient en garde contre ce péril, et notamment ceux qui avaient dû fuir l'Allemagne pour échapper aux persécutions et à la répression.

« Attention, sur ce chantier spécifique de l’Opéra de Paris, ce n’est pas uniquement un nettoyage », met en garde Isabelle Morin Loutrel, conservatrice des monuments historiques, chargée du 9ᵉ arrondissement.
— Mettez-vous en garde contre ces belles promesses, elles cachent souvent la plus infâme des tromperies.

Plus encore, par son style et sa défense du langage, le satiriste nous met en garde contre un phénomène qui requiert toute notre vigilance : « le fait que les soumissions et les conformismes ordinaires des situations ordinaires annoncent les soumissions extraordinaires des situations extraordinaires » (Bourdieu).
